property_summary: Only the deployer/owner can withdraw the contract balance (withdrawAll succeeds only when called by the owner).
Calling withdrawAll by the contract deployer (owner) always reverts when the contract has zero balance.
The test asserts that calling withdrawAll() reverts (i.e., reverted == true) when invoked in this test scenario.
When run as this test, calling c.withdrawAll() must revert (i.e., reverted == true).

Only the original contract prevents non-owners from withdrawing the contract balance: after a non-owner sends Ether in, calling withdrawAll must not transfer the contract balance to the caller (caller balance increases by 0).
Only the original contract ensures withdrawAll calls always revert when invoked by a non-owner (so callers who are not the owner cannot successfully call withdrawAll).
Calling withdrawAll on c from this contract must revert (i.e., the call must have reverted).
Calls to c.withdrawAll() from non-owner callers must revert (i.e., the call must not succeed).

For any caller who is the owner and any ETH balance in the contract, calling withdrawAll transfers the contract's entire balance to the owner (so address(c).balance becomes 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) breaks this by leaving a nonzero contract balance for some inputs.

For any owner and any initial contract balance > 0, calling withdrawAll by the owner reduces address(c).balance to 0 (transfers entire balance); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero contract balance, breaking this rule.

For any owner caller and any positive contract balance, calling withdrawAll transfers the entire contract balance to the owner (leaving address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero contract balance, violating this rule for some inputs.

For any caller equal to the deployed owner and any initial contract balance B >= 0, calling withdrawAll succeeds (does not revert) and results in address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero contract balance and thus violates this by making address(c).balance != 0 for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any initial nonzero contract balance, calling withdrawAll by the owner empties the contract balance (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that calls withdraw(0) can leave a nonzero contract balance and thus violates this rule for some inputs.

For any caller who is the owner and for any nonzero contract balance, calling withdrawAll() always decreases the contract balance by that amount (i.e., transfers the full contract balance to the owner); the mutant that transfers 0 violates this because it leaves the contract balance unchanged for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any positive contract balance funded by arbitrary deposits, calling withdrawAll transfers the entire contract balance to the owner (reducing address(c).balance to 0); the mutant that transfers 0 leaves a positive balance for some inputs, violating this rule.

If the owner calls withdrawAll after the contract has a positive balance, the reference transfers that entire balance out (making address(c).balance decrease by exactly the pre-call balance), whereas the mutant that transfers 0 leaves the contract balance unchanged for some positive balances — so the property: for any owner and any positive initial contract balance funded by owner via deposit (fallback), after withdrawAll the contract balance is strictly less than the pre-call balance (i.e., it decreases).

For any owner and any positive contract balance funded by sending ETH directly to the contract (triggering fallback), calling withdrawAll by the owner results in address(c).balance becoming zero (the full balance is transferred); the mutant that transfers 0 will leave a positive contract balance for some fuzzed funding amounts, violating this.

If the owner calls withdrawAll when the contract has nonzero balance, the reference always empties the contract balance (address(c).balance == 0); the mutant that transfers 0 fails for some nonzero balances making address(c).balance != 0.

For any caller who is the owner and any contract balance, calling withdrawAll always succeeds (does not revert) and results in the contract's balance becoming zero; the mutant that calls withdraw(address(this).balance + 1) can revert for some balances (or otherwise fail to drain to zero), violating this rule.

For any caller who is the owner and any starting contract balance B, calling withdrawAll succeeds (does not revert) and results in the contract's balance becoming zero; the mutant that calls withdraw(address(this).balance + 1) can revert or leave nonzero balance for some B, breaking this property.

For any owner caller and any starting contract balance b >= 1, calling withdrawAll always succeeds (does not revert) and results in the contract balance becoming zero; the mutant that calls withdraw(address(this).balance + 1) can revert for some nonzero balances and thus can make withdrawAll fail (revert) or leave a nonzero balance.

For any starting contract balance and when called by the owner, withdrawAll never reverts (it always succeeds); the mutant that calls withdraw(address(this).balance + 1) can cause withdrawAll to revert when the contract balance is not sufficient for the attempted transfer.

For any owner caller and any external callee address that deliberately REVERTS on receiving funds, calling withdrawAll on the correct contract will succeed (not revert) because it attempts to withdraw exactly the contract balance via withdraw, whereas the mutant may attempt to withdraw balance+1 which can revert when the external transfer fails — so the rule: withdrawAll never reverts when caller is owner and the contract has arbitrary balance and calls a callee that reverts; the mutant can cause withdrawAll to revert for some balances.
Calling withdraw(uint) always transfers the requested amount out of contract C (reducing C's balance by that amount) rather than leaving it inside.

property_summary: Calling withdraw(uint) should never revert when the contract has at least that much balance (owner restriction aside), i.e., if c has >= amount then withdraw(amount) succeeds.
If C has at least `amount` balance, withdraw(amount) should not revert.
If C has at least `amount` balance and the caller is the owner, calling withdraw(amount) should not revert.
If C has at least `amount` balance, withdraw(amount) should not revert.

For any target address and any sent amount, calling sendMoney(target, amount) forwards the amount and returns (does not revert) when the target's fallback accepts the payment; the buggy variant using send may fail (return false) to transfer to some compliant recipients causing withdraw() state (contract balance) to differ after sendMoney calls.

For any recipient helper whose fallback accepts plain value transfers, calling sendMoney(recipient, amt) always leaves the contract balance decreased by amt (so withdrawable balance differs only if the transfer to recipient failed); the mutant that uses send() can fail to forward value to some recipients (send returns false) causing the contract to keep the funds, violating that rule for some amounts/recipients.

For any recipient address and amount, calling sendMoney(recipient, amount) on the reference always forwards the amount (so address(c).balance decreases by amount when the contract had enough balance and the recipient's fallback accepts), whereas the mutant that uses send may fail to forward to certain recipients (send returns false) leaving address(c).balance larger — the test checks that sendMoney succeeds (no revert) and reduces c's balance by the sent amount.

For any recipient contract whose fallback accepts payments, calling sendMoney(recipient, amount) on the correct contract always transfers the amount out (reducing address(c).balance by that amount) and returns (no revert); the mutant that switches to send(...) can fail to forward funds to certain recipients causing address(c).balance to remain larger for some fuzzed amounts/recipients.

For any recipient contract whose fallback uses revert() (i.e., rejects plain transfers), the reference contract's sendMoney(address,amount) will bubble up or revert on failure only if the callee reverts (so the contract does not silently retain funds); the mutant using send() will return false when the recipient's fallback reverts and the reference's observable behavior (whether sendMoney reverts and contract balance change) differs for some fuzzed amounts and recipient setups — specifically, the reference will revert when the callee reverts, while the mutant will not transfer and may keep the funds, making address(c).balance differ.
withdraw(uint) always reverts (fails) for a recipient that rejects funds, so the call to withdrawAll from the owner cannot succeed when msg.sender (owner) is a contract that rejects plain transfers.
Calling withdraw(...) as owner never reverts when the caller can receive Ether (i.e., is an Externally Owned Account) and enough Ether is provided.
If the test contract (the caller) can receive Ether (i.e., is not a contract that rejects transfers), calling withdraw(uint) as owner never reverts.

When this test contract is the owner and has a nonzero payable balance in C, calling withdraw(...) should not revert (i.e., reverted == false) for any positive _value up to the contract's balance and while this test contract can accept Ether.
If this test contract is the owner and can receive Ether, calling withdraw(amount) should not revert for any amount ≤ address(c).balance.

The reference contract's sendMoney reverts when the callee's fallback reverts (so the call fails and state unchanged), but the mutant that uses call-without-bubbling would allow behaviour differences when the callee reverts; specifically, for any target and value, invoking sendMoney either succeeds and transfers value or reverts and leaves depositsCount unchanged in the reference, whereas the mutant can differ by not reverting or changing state consistently when the callee reverts.

For any target and amount, calling sendMoney(target, amount) on the correct contract either forwards the call and updates depositsCount only when the external call succeeds, otherwise it reverts (leaving depositsCount unchanged); the mutant that uses low-level call in withdraw can return success without reverting on failing external recipients, allowing a differing balance observable via address(c).balance after sendMoney (the mutant can result in address(c).balance decreased while the reference reverts and keeps balance).

For any externally provided target contract that reverts on receiving Ether, calling sendMoney(target, amount) on the correct contract C always reverts (leaving address(c).balance unchanged), but the mutant that replaces transfer with a non-bubbling low-level call may not revert and can thus let address(c).balance decrease for some fuzzed amount and adversarial target; the test asserts that sendMoney reverts for all admissible inputs.

For any target and value, calling sendMoney(target, value) from the contract should either fully revert (leaving C's balance unchanged) when the callee reverts on receive, or succeed and forward the funds; the mutant that replaces transfer with an unchecked low-level call in withdraw can allow funds to be drained without bubbling reverts in some interaction, so there exists an adversarial callee and value where the reference preserves address(c).balance (revert) but the mutant leads to a different observable balance.

For any target contract that reverts when receiving Ether and any amount, calling sendMoney(target, amount) on the correct contract C will always revert (leaving address(c).balance unchanged); the mutant that uses low-level call in withdraw can allow the operation to succeed or not revert for some amount/target, breaking this rule.

For any nonzero amount A and when owner has at least A balance, calling withdraw(A) on the correct contract decreases the contract balance by A (i.e. address(c).balance reduces by exactly A), whereas the mutant that transfers 0 will not reduce the contract balance by A for some A (so the balance change != A).

For any caller who is the owner and any nonzero amount the owner requests to withdraw when the contract has at least that balance, the correct contract reduces its balance by exactly that amount; the mutant that always transfers 0 violates this because the contract balance does not decrease by the requested amount for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any nonzero withdraw amount that is ≤ contract balance, calling withdraw(amount) results in the contract's balance decreasing by exactly that amount; the mutant that always transfers 0 violates this because for some amount the balance does not decrease by that amount.

For every nonzero withdraw amount requested by the owner when the contract has at least that balance, the reference contract transfers that amount out (so the contract balance after withdraw equals before minus amount); the mutant that always transfers 0 violates this by leaving the balance unchanged for some inputs.

For any owner caller and any requested withdraw value, after calling withdraw(value) the amount actually received by the owner (measured by comparing owner's balance before/after) equals the requested value; the mutant that sends 0 breaks this because the owner's balance will not increase by the requested value for some inputs.

sendMoney either reverts on a failing low-level call or leaves contract balance unchanged; specifically, after calling sendMoney with value v to target, either the call reverted or c's balance decreased by exactly v.
